item.title: Tales of Archivist Tündér
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: Tale

Genre: Drama/Emotional & History

Elevator Pitch: An expansion upon the lore of Alexandria Eternal, the staff working on the project, the character of Alexandria Eternal itself, and the exploration of the history of Alexandria Eternal as well as the limits and bounds of what can be contained within the shelves of Alexandria Eternal.

Central Narrative: The main focus on this tale will be Archivist Tündér's experiences, project logs, and experiments performed within or related to Alexandria Eternal.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Archivist's Tündér's excitement, expectations, and experiences on the first time they entered Alexandria Eternal.

Additional Notes: Later on I will expand on Archivist Tündér's lore by showing how she moved up from the digitization of old handwritten SCP articles to suggesting testing that had yet to be attempted on various SCPs she became aware of as part of the digitization project and how her successful or enlightening testing suggestions earned her security clearance level 4 and the position of digitization lead on the SCP 4001 team.

item.title: Re: The Ophanim
item.content:encoded:
In general: The concept kept me going, and the pacing is okay. The dialogue is fine, but the description gets in the way during the logs. There is a large amount of conflicting or unexplained information that makes following the article difficult. That's mostly outside of the logs that you're worried about. The logs themselves have a lot of problems with tone.

Here are my thoughts and recommendations, roughly in order:

Object classification: This is the first and will probably be the last time I have ever recommend this, but given that this thing is causing an ongoing, unstoppable and exponentially increasing worldwide rapture… We're probably beyond Keter. I don't know what the fancy apocalypse object class du jour is these days, but I would recommend dialing the sheer scope of your SCP back if you don't want to deal with the scrutiny that comes with a zany object class.

+ SCProcedures
- SCProcedures

Physical containment of SCP-XXXX is impossible.

This is not worth including.

Several Mark II Self-Sustaining Cumulous Steam Generators (SSCSG) are to orbit around SCP-XXXX. Meteorological data is to be fed to each SSCSG in order to maintain a thick cloud around SCP-XXXX.

Mostly good, "thick cloud" doesn't seem clinical enough in tone.

Outside containment consultants, as well as several members of GOI-### ("The Horizon Initiative") have been contracted to isolate the region of the Noosphere containing concepts of and relating to SCP-XXXX.

It's a small o in GoI.

I took a brief look around the site and apparently it's established enough that a handful of articles use it freely with no context, but I spent a good chunk of this article wondering if you were ever going to explain what the Noosphere was. After Googling it, I spent the rest of the time wondering why we were glossing over the metaphysical concept of the collective unconscious being a physical space that an MTF can just stroll on into.

This is probably going to tie into most other places where I was confused. If there's a master definition of this somewhere, it should be linked and embedded since it's crucial to following the plot of your article.

Additionally, the final log makes it seem like XXXX got bodied all the way out of the Noosphere. The Horizon Initiative contracting already occurred, and doesn't seem like it has any bearing on the current containment procedures.

Foundation agents embedded in religious organizations are to pursuade as many followers into worship of SCP-XXXX as possible.

Persuade. Also, why?

The following phrase is to be repeated by those participating in the containment of SCP-XXXX:

> Be not afraid.

Repeated how? In what way? At specific times? Participating in the containment under what conditions? Also, again, why?

The article does not make it clear, and it also makes the later shift of Raynes' name to the phrase confusing. To be honest, it doesn't serve much purpose in either instance—it's just here because you know those wacky Abrahamic Angels and their catchphrase, they just feel bad about being so goshdarn spooky.

+ Description
- Description

Whether or not the flame is responsible for SCP-XXXX's ability to remain airborne is unclear.

There's no particular reason to think this, and this line doesn't add anything.

Also: Do you need a reason to justify remaining airborne in the metaphysical concept of the collective unconsciousness?

At this time, there is no method of preventing a Pencerahan Event, or ceasing one in progress.

Sure there is: the description says it only works on people who are aware of SCP-XXXX. You can prevent it by making sure they don't know about it. Actually, given that, shouldn't the instructions in the SCProcedures be to convince as many people as possible to stop worshiping SCP-XXXX? Or to try and axe the Abrahamic faiths entirely?

Actually, this thing isn't God, it's God's hype man for the rapture. I haven't been to church in quite a while, but you don't really worship angels, right?

A pile of salt
A pile of ash
Brimstone

I like where this ends up going. I don't think it needs to be rendered in bullet points, however. That just makes it distracting. "Transform" and "piles of" also aren't terribly clinical.

The description seems inconsistent on whether they just turn into salt or burn alive. I would recommend uniformly burning alive, and something to the effect of "leaving behind trace elements of either carbon, sodium or sulfur."

(In footnote 3) All Foundation staff that participated in this experiment expressed disgust and concern for the D-Class once it had concluded. Several resigned.

Your Foundation personnel are babies. Especially given that people are apparently getting unwillingly raptured worldwide and the nature of their entire job and organization is to prevent and contain paranormal events. Burning up some convicts for the greater good hardly seems like it should be the barf-inducing final straw.

The actual table looks fine (I would still recommend the change to "carbon, sodium or sulfur" so that it's not so in-your-face that they're going straight to the Actual Abrahamic Hell That Exists). You do use "turns" instead of "turned" a handful of times.

Since you're leaning into religious imagery here: All the people with really severe crimes going to hell is straightforward. Adding a note in there about someone with a prior history of murder who has displayed conversion to a life of faith turning into salt, or someone who committed minor crimes but never repented turning into brimstone would go a long way towards giving this article more depth.

Pencerahan Events

The language on which thing causes what was already a bit confusing, but this one drives it home. At different points in the article, we have these descriptions:

1. When people directly view SCP-XXXX, they confess their sins and then explode.
2. When people are told SCP-XXXX exists, but don't directly view it, they cannot tell a lie, develop peace and good will about mankind, man, and then turn into salt, uniformly (apparently learning about it but not seeing it means you go up instead of down).
3. When people are "aware" of it, but don't know it exists, they have an emotional breakdown, strip, and then pelvic-thrust into the sky. This is different from being told it exists, for reasons that are unclear.

You need to clarify these concepts and marry them together. I personally don't think the concept of a Pencerahan Event as described actually adds anything here. You seem attached to the term, so you could consider using it for the ongoing worldwide rapture occurring in the article, instead of each individual that gets raptured. I think getting raptured or exploding into heaven/hell/purgatory substance should all just be considered and logged as potential effects of exposure.

+ The Logs
- The Logs

You need more context for these. The fact that people are getting raptured left and right feels like an End-of-the-World Scenario, but it's glossed over. A vague percentage, the difficulty in containment, the ticking clock that billions will burn alive and throw the world into chaos—drive that home. Make us believe the Foundation would be willing to break the wheels of the chariot of God to save humanity. Ignoring Secure and Contain in order to Protect is a big step you cannot skip over if the Foundation has decided to merc an anomaly.

MTF Zeta-9 (Mole Rats)

They do specialize in places that don't follow normal physics and space/time, and I'm assuming the improbably physical nature of the Noosphere has some of that going on. But it never actually comes up during the article, so it feels like you just included them because they're the neat ones people like.

(I am people. God bless our scuttling bois, the Mole Rats are my favorites. <3)

<Begin Log>

The actual dialogue in this section is fine.

The descriptions at times stray from clinical, but that is tricky to fix while still describing a Spooky Abrahamic Angel. Most of my problems aren't in this one.

Someone in the background expresses disapproval, but what is said is unheard.

"Unintelligible" would be a better word choice, but things like this are always a little awkward to include in logs.

Foxtrot steps into the fire and is consumed by it. She does not scream.

This one's probably the least clinical line in this log. You could just cut it down to "Foxtrot steps into the fire." Remember, this is for professional purposes—if the Foundation is writing it, it's not going to be anything but bare-bones descriptive.

Containment Consultant Meeting

In attendance: O5-7, Researcher Raynes

Also, this Woo person.

O5-7: Now, before we begin I feel that it is imperative that we-

Raynes: Xir, with all due respect

I feel like cutting off an O5 at a professional meeting with another GoI should get you fired. Into the sun.

O5-7: Take some time off, doctor. I need you level headed for what's to come next.

Why does it have to be Raynes? After that outburst, it feels like they should have picked someone else. An event this large cannot have only Raynes working on it as a researcher. There is no compelling reason presented to use someone who is emotionally unstable and bearing the guilt of multiple deaths while the fate of humanity is at stake.

you mind giving us some elucidation

This is a really strange turn of phrase.

U-90 Alpha fires at it to no avail. U-90 Beta and Raynes attempt to flee but are unable to get passed the Horizon Initative.

"No avail" doesn't seem clinical. You meant "past."

Immediately following tge Initiative's egress from the Noosphere, an unknown entity manifested below SCP-XXXX.

Okay, the Noosphere is not on Earth, even if it's a physical place. Woo even refers to it as the theoretical realm. How do they know what happened in the Noosphere after the Initiative left?

The unknown entity was roughly humanoid, and had innumerable wings that allowed it to maintain self-sustained flight. The entity had several thousand faces as well, and each of it's wings were lined with eyes.

Getting too flowery. Not clinical enough.

The unknown entity elevated upward, knocking SCP-XXXX into the stratosphere.

Wait, so you can punch something out of the collective unconscious?

…That's honestly badass, but it probably bears more description that Raynes turned into a megazord and punched the Chariot of God into another dimension.

Despite the overwhelming evidence supporting the existence of 'Researcher Raynes', there are no records in file of any Foundation personnel bearing that moniker.

Are there no records or is there overwhelming evidence? Where's the discrepancy? This doesn't feel like it ties into anything at all.

Following Incident T-2:1-10, the name 'Raynes' exhibits a mild anti-memetic effect, rendering anyone unable to vocalize it. When subjects attempt to speak the word 'Raynes', they instead speak the phrase 'Be not afraid.'.

I'm pretty sure that's a memetic effect, not an anti-memetic effect. Also, the logistics of not being able to say the name "Raynes" is non-trivial. (For one, you'd never be able to sing Africa again.) Consider making that effect apply to the full name only.

+ Overall Suggestions
- Overall Suggestions

Procedures: These are largely fine, but could use a little tidying up for tone and clarity. The "Be Not Afraid" thing is confusing and doesn't add much. The bit about worshiping SCP-XXXX makes no sense.

Description: You need to pin down the effects of this thing and make them feel consistent. The ideas are neat, with some tweaking so they're a little less on the nose. As it is, they're contradictory and that needs to be resolved.

As sold as I am on the concept of punching God's Secretary of Rapture into another dimension, I don't think the Noosphere actually adds anything to the article. I haven't been keeping close tabs on the wiki over the past ~2 years as it's continued to blow up, so it's possible I am the last person here to learn about the Noosphere. For my money at least, all it does is make the article vastly more confusing.

It's a really big concept to introduce if you're not going to use it, and to be honest, you don't. They go into the Noosphere, yes—they could just as easily go to whatever physical location the Ophanim parked itself on, it doesn't really make a difference to the story structure. It has a cognitohazardous effect that reaches people through the Noosphere, yes. You could also just have that be a thing that it does from wherever it's sitting on Earth. Since it seems like the Mole Rats go in there and die (as my poor scuttly bois are wont to do), with their physical bodies, there's no unorthodox ramifications to dying in the Noosphere. There's no strange topography or space/time shenanigans due to its presence in the story.

I recommend hacking it out entirely. If you're not willing to do so, I would recommend making it more clear what the Noosphere is, and why it's crucial to the article and nature of the anomaly.

The Logs: Your dialogue is fine (give or take that I think Raynes shouldn't be able to mouth off to an O5). The descriptions need to be a bit more clinical, and the last one needs to be much more clinical if you want it to be a Foundation document.

This is a suggestion, but given the tone in the last Incident Log, and that it concerns events that it seems like only the Horizon Initiative could have witnessed. Instead of being presented as official Foundation documentation, it could be a personal document submitted by the Initiative (or Woo personally) as a description for the Foundation files.

If you want to keep the idea that the Foundation has somehow forgotten he exists, you can then follow that up with the gut-punch: Despite the previous correspondence from Woo, the Foundation has no personnel records for a Researcher of that name. Video logs, likewise provided by the Horizon Initiative, have been recorded on equipment that matches Foundation standard body cameras. However, the footage frequently cuts out and is replaced with a black screen, with white text that reads "BE NOT AFRAID."

That said, the Foundation forgetting Raynes exists but not SCP-XXXX doesn't make a whole lot of sense for that ending. There's nothing that alludes to the COB burning him out of the Foundation personnel files, and it doesn't match up to the behavior of SCP-XXXX. If that's the ultimate role of the Noosphere in this story, somehow, it needs to be made clear.

Overall, the idea is neat and you sold me pretty heavily on suplexing an angel into low-space, but it needs cleaning, technically and conceptually. You also need to pin down the timeline of what happens when. The early portions of the article make it sound like the rapture is still happening, the last logs seem to imply it's over and just needs some clouds sprayed on it to keep it contained. With revision, this could be great.

item.title: Re: So Let It Be Written, So Let It Be Done
item.content:encoded:
Got a PM about this, took a look.

I'll admit, the hook being "So let it be written, so let it be done". rather than intrigue me, makes me as a reader immediately skeptical. Written works manifesting into the real world, with accompanying (in)convenient memory-affecting effects, aren't really new or interesting so far as stories on the mainsite and popular media go (the first example that comes to mind for me is the Book of Ages from Jackie Chan Adventures: https://jackiechanadventures.fandom.com/wiki/Book_of_Ages / https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aga4_I1PZKI). The fact that yours is a lithostone that relies on existing written material makes this even more questionable to me as a reader; mostly because I've seen plenty of variations of the same sort of item used to bring characters and items from series like Harry Potter to life in the real world (and also the potential issue of readers, especially our international bilingual community, not being immediately familiar with works like Swift's A Modest Proposal).

Personally I feel like if you really want to make this work on the mainsite, you should revise it into a tale or Group of Interest format so there's more focus on the narrative behind both the bookbinders and whatever group is trying to figure out what they're doing. The core anomaly of "mess with writing, real life is messed with" isn't something that interests me after I've seen it attempted so many times, and what's presented here doesn't divert from the usual approach enough to convince me it'll be unique.

I myself feel like you'd get more positive readership if you introduce some characters whose struggles the audience can relate more with (probably the original owners of the anomaly… though ideally you'd also freshen up the worldbuilding so the acquisition of the item isn't just left to essentially dumb luck and the convenience of the item falling into the hands of someone who will conveniently use it so the effects can conveniently manifest). Then follow those characters through the story, rather than focusing on the lithostone. The Foundation itself barely features in the story anyway; I think it's better to focus on the good portions of the narrative rather than shoehorn the Foundation in. Tales like The Orb is the Key and The Worm might be a good start for guidance/inspiration.

item.title: Re: Lost in the Fog / Temporal SCP
item.content:encoded:
I'm not normally a critiquer, so take this with a rather large grain of salt:

+ Line Critique
- Line Critique

I'm sure a lot of this is super pedantic, so I have given each critique a pedantry rating. "Important" means I think it might be an issue, "Medium" means it could go either way, "Nitpick" means it's such a small and pedantic critique that it probably doesn't matter too much.

A Foundation meteorological team is to be stationed at Site-287 at all times, which is to receive additional staffing during the spring and autumn.

To avoid the double “is to” thing you get when combining these ideas, you could try “A Foundation meteorological team is to be stationed at Site-287 at all times, with additional staffing during the spring and autumn.”

Rating: Medium

…under the premise…

You probably meant “…under the pretense…”

Rating: Nitpick

…until the anomaly has dissipated.

If the cause of this is an event (a NOTD event), the procedure should last “…until the event has completed.”

Rating: Nitpick

…all personnel are restricted from entering SCP-XXXX…

SCP-XXXX isn't one constant thing, it's a designation of a manifestation, so that should be reflected here as "…all personnel are restricted from entering SCP-XXXX manifestations…"

Rating: Medium

…colloquially referred to as missing time…

…I just thought this was a strange detail to include. Why do we care what the locals call it, especially when what they call it doesn't give us any new information? If the name was some important local cultural thing, or if it gave us a subtle hint to the nature of the origin of the anomaly, maybe this could be important. But as it stands, it's just distracting.

Rating: Medium

…was less than 2.5 °C (4.5 °F).

The imperial numbers in parenthesis thing is really only for when precision is needed, so with "less than" and with the two values not being exactly the same, it's not really necessary.

Rating: Nitpick

Any trespassers are usually apprehended, questioned, and then given Class-B amnestics before being released.

Why only usually? That should probably just be standard procedure for all trespassers.

Rating: Medium

- Line Critique
+ Block Critique
- Block Critique

ConProcs

This is the part of the article I think I found most issue with. Simply put, I don't find that the article has justified these containment procedures. For example, why does the foundation spend so much effort to find out exactly when another manifestation will occur? Wouldn't it be easier for them to just shut down the whole road for the spring and autumn months, rather than using an entire meteorological team plus extra staff? I feel like a bimonthly security perimeter makes just as much sense, and be lower maintenance. Perhaps the current ConProcs would make more sense if the anomaly was more erratic in it's timing, but it's presented as quite regular.

- Block Critique

I guess the fact that I didn't find much at all wrong with the second half of the article must mean I was pretty invested! And yeah, the stinger at the end was great. Overall, I don't have too much to say, mostly because I think it's just about ready. Good luck to you!

item.title: Reanimating Elephant Graveyards
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: No

Page Type: SCP Article

Page Layout (Optional): Mostly the usual shtick, might include interview logs and/or discovery logs. This part isn't fleshed out yet and can still change a lot.

Elevator Pitch: All elephant graveyards are anomalous, the skeletons in them inevitably coming to live every 40-70 years. The living dead results reassemble themselves in a humanoid shape and move in a specific direction for 15 minutes before then falling apart again and repeating the process 40-70 years later.
The place they are moving towards is an obscure part of Russia where other elephant skeletons have already been stacked up many meters high in an intricate shape.
There also may be a secondary effect to the living skeletons that causes people to hallucinate, blurring the details of the encounter.

Central Narrative: No concrete narrative but rather the idea that the public is aware of the elephant skeletons, considering them an urban legend. The foundation would then have to base its procedures on that fact and make sure the people believe the scp to be a hoax.
The event's age would also be explored as parallels are drawn between it and cave drawings or alleged cyclops encounters.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The main hook would be the vague knowledge that the public has of the scp, as well as the weirdness of the event itself. Similar ideas have been made into scps before but I believe that the specifics make my concept stand out among the others.

Additional Notes: The whole "humanoid elephant skeleton" idea is largely based on the theory that people used to mistake elephant skulls for those of cyclopes, creating that myth in the first place.
Specific numbers and values were mostly chosen to make the scp as annoying to contain as possible(a bit silly in hindsight).
I know that the idea still needs a good amount of polishing. I hope I can turn it into something sort of worthwhile in the end.

item.title: The Rube Effect
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Drama/Emotional, Comedy

Page Layout: Test and incident logs to be included. I intend to cross refence other works, but would like to ask permission from other authors before I commit to that.

Elevator Pitch: Woman is infected with a "virus" of sorts that neutralizes nearby deadly threats with 'events' that work on a similar principle to the butterfly effect or a Rube Goldberg machine. It can manipulate any non-organic material to complete an event. The woman is incredulously unaware of her anomalous properties.

Central Narrative: The virus is contagious but this is unknown by the Foundation at the time of the article's writing. Its effects are efficient but subtle. The Subject was the child of two researchers who were killed in a containment breach. She's sent to live at the School for Children of Prominence. A boarding school/orphanage for children of Foundation personnel. She is notably idiotic and it amazes her teachers that she actually graduates. Once she starts working for the Foundation as a junior researcher, her peers are dumbfounded that despite lacking all common sense she has yet to die. This prompts an investigation and her eventual classification as an SCP. After the article is submitted for review the higher ups begin to doubt the judgement of the lead researcher and try to have the SCP declassified due to 'lack or sufficient anomalous evidence'. The lead researcher is shunned and dives into a depressed drunken stupor. It remains to be seen if the Foundation will continue the research and discover how to harness the power of this virus.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The virus isn't all powerful and it wont infect just anyone. It's host can still be injured and it will not prevent death due to biological means such as old age or venom. It is, however, very good at keeping its host alive. The Foundation would kill to have something like this for all of their field agents.

item.title: Yay cactusposting :D
item.content:encoded:
So glad to see this here, it's super fun!

Of course, I'll always have nitpicks
But the overall here is great!

…and the ability to increase and decrease height in levitation.

Strange phrasing here. Maybe you wanted "…and the ability to increase and decrease the height at which it's levitating."

Page Layout (optional): Contains containment procedures, description, discovery, test logs, and maybe even a cross-link.

Elevator Pitch: A “living” carved wooden vulture that feeds on human corpses. It will get “hungry” after 24 hours, which is when it will start searching for corpses to feed on. If it hasn't eaten for 36 to 48 hours, it will enter a frenzy, which makes it exponentially stronger and more aggressive. In this state, it will eat people alive in order to satiate its “hunger.” In this state, it will even ignore any dead human meat and go straight for the nearest living human.

Central Narrative: What is speculated to be its first victim was a woodworker specializing in custom statues. It's believed that the vulture killed the victim as opposed to feasting on their corpse.

Ever since the first body was found, mutilated and dismembered, many more bodies soon popped up with similar disfigurements. This caused many problems for local law enforcement.

The Foundation stepped in when a video of the creature was brought into the hands of the police. What caught their eye was the unnatural material it seemed to be made out of.

The Foundation easily caught it with the scent of human flesh, but they did not fully understand its eating habits at the time, nor did they anticipate the consequences of the lack of understanding that they had. They tried to feed it animal carcasses. They were able to keep it for 2 days before it escaped in one of its “frenzy states” and ate a facility guard alive. It was soon recaptured and given human flesh to eat. It hasn't escaped, nor tried to escape since then.

Presently, the SCP sits in its containment cell, docile. It is given a pound of human flesh every 24 hours. It seems to be satiated.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The simple but unique appearance and description combined with the grotesque nature of its feeding.

Additional Notes: “How's The Foundation able to obtain the human flesh that they feed the SCP?”

The Foundation has struck a deal with a nearby city using one of their front companies, which allows them access to unwanted or unclaimed dead bodies. They also have access to the corpses of people who have donated their bodies to science.

I’d be willing to delete the “escaped and ate a guard” part to make The Foundation not look like idiots.

If this ever gets greenlit I’d like to include a brief cross-link to SCP-3847 if possible.

item.title: Re: Tale - MTF Agents Investigate An Anomaly
item.content:encoded:
Okay, so I know you're mostly looking for smoke checks on grammar, and I'll get to that. I'm gonna drop some nested critique first though.

+ Feedback
- Feedback

I like a lot of the central ideas here, looking at the slightly bigger picture of what you're going for in the ideas thread, this seems like it could be a neat series once it's more fleshed out.

I have some issues with the structure and pacing. There's a lot of banter between Rodney and Polk, and it's broken up by descriptions of their behavior, which can be good. But that's all those descriptions are doing. The narration isn't underscoring or adding to the conversation or making us more familiar with these characters, beyond them being tired field agents. They have a bit of difference in their personalities, but the way they speak and some of the actions they're taking feel a bit too similar. It seems like you want them to have a buddy-cop vibe. For the sake of that, describing them more in appearance, making their mannerisms more distinct and giving their statements more context could be very helpful.

For instance, Rodney seems more philosophical and laidback. Polk seems a bit more clinical and by-the-book. I like the contrast of the more uptight character wanting to be a deskjockey with the easygoing character wanting to be the rough-and-tumble field agent. While it makes some sense for the scene, introducing both of these characters jamming food into their mouths makes them feel too similar. With no description of what they look like, or how they act beyond their immediate actions, they muddy together a bit too much.

This extends further: Diva-Scent is a teenage girl (if you're not inoculated against memes). That's a broad category! How does she dress? How does she look? How does she behave? The slight valley girl edge comes through in her dialogue, but it's not enough on its own.

Story note: Polk really took his partner not being immunized against memetics in stride when they're clearly about to go deal with a memetic effect they don't understand. Diva-Scent's appearance even carries through electronic media, apparently. Since Polk seems more uptight (and is looking for an excuse to get out of more dangerous fieldwork), it sticks out as odd that he'd just go "Oh, okay, you're putting both of us in danger while we approach an event we don't understand," without even letting dispatch know. For the sake of the story, I would consider having your trash crew look human on film, even to someone who's inoculated. That way, by the time your characters realize it's important that Rodney isn't immune to that effect, they're already in the area and dealing with the situation.

A couple of times, you gloss over things that feel like they should be more descriptive. Polk and Rodney realizing they're seeing two different things is one of those times. That feels like it should be focused on in character instead of glossed over in a sentence. There's also very little scene setting in places where it feels like it should be important—I had to reread multiple times to understand that there wasn't any trash when they arrived to the area the volunteers had been cleaning up.

Last mild quibbles on writing style:

-You can just say "Rodney said" or "Polk said." A big chunk of the dialogue is rendered like "Polk improvised" or "Rodney interrupted." Reserve the more specific words for places where they're needed, to make them impactful instead of distracting.

-You use the word "apparently" a lot while directly describing something—you don't need to do that, you're already telling us exactly what's happening as the narrator. You can use "apparently" when it's something the narrator is alluding to. Example: If you are describing a car crash, describe the car crash. If you're describing two wrecked cars on the side of the road, then you can say "Apparently, there had been a car crash."

-This is personal preference, but I recommend avoiding ellipses as much as possible. Places where you would put ellipses are generally better served by including more description or restructuring the flow of dialogue to avoid them entirely. If you're going to use ellipses, use them at the end or beginning of dialogue to indicate awkward pauses or speech fading in or out as the description demands.

-If you can, read your dialogue out loud and see if it feels natural. Several portions (particularly when they speak to the teens) feel a bit awkward and stilted.

For notes on errors and specific recommendations:

+ Errors
- Errors

Agent Rodney chuckled at Polk "You can eat once you're off duty; that's field work." Into the mic now, "Dispatch, what do you got?"

Missing a period. I'd recommend against the semicolon. That goes for the rest of the semicolons, but it's particularly distracting when it's in dialogue. "Into the mic now," is a bit awkward, particularly since you never stated he was off-mic to begin with.

"Guys, this garbage strike is really just too much. I'm standing here on 10th street downtown, and there is ssooo much trash everywhere!"

Recommend using one s and italicizing the sooo for emphasis.

"My memetic immunizations aren't current," Rodney explained away the awkward moment

I already mentioned that I recommend rewriting this. As it is though, terminate the dialogue with a period since you're describing what happens after Rodney says that, not what's happening along with it.

The crowd was gradually beginning to disperse, their work apparently done.

Just pointing this sentence out as an acceptable use of "apparently," good job.

They picked out a group of three young men who were still lingering; one of them still had coveralls and gloves on.

You're setting up Coveralls as the character used for dialogue in this scene. That fragment after the semicolon is awkward, though. I'd recommend mentioning the coveralls to make him stick out once he's already started speaking.

Probably assessing whether these two were cops or not, thought Rodney.

Since it's Rodney's thought, he should probably be thinking "whether we're cops or not."

"Like… Ok, so I guess lots of old folks live in some of these apartments?"

Spell out "okay." You do this a few more times later.

He added with a shrug, "so that sucks."

"He added with a shrug" reads like it should come after a line and not before it. Try "With a shrug, he added" instead.

The most important note is that you switch from past to present tense:

Scanning the surrounding area, none of the accumulated garbage remains

Here.

Finally they see it, like a line drawn at the mouth of an alleyway…

And then for the rest of the story from this line. Unless it's part of an intentional framing device, don't switch the tenses of the narrator. Past tense is the usual standard in fiction.

"Sir, can you turn that engine off for a minute!"

Might be personal preference, since he is shouting, but the exclamation point feels like it should be a question mark.

All four men have the exact same thought,

Punctuate this with a period after fixing the change in tense.

Since some of that might seem harsh: I want to emphasize that I'm completely on board for this idea. I think there's room for sillier premises on the site, especially in Tales. Stephen King's Trucks, mixed with a heist movie and a femme fatale talking garbage can is the kind of bonkers I can get behind. I'd be happy to take another look at this after you've cleaned up some errors and punched up the dialogue and description a bit.

Summoned via PM:

Hi again MisterNightmare013. Let’s take a look at your new concept.

Okay, much as I empathise with your (probably) Asian upbringing, I don’t see this working as a scip. For one, you’re basing the scp off demanding parents – why are they considered anomalous? My own mother uses the phrase “You grew up to be such a disappointment” on a weekly basis on me. It’s how Asian parents are. Furthermore, you seem to be hinting at a compulsion effect that strongly creates feelings of disappointment and paralysis in the scp’s victims. Most of the modern scips frown upon these effects – it feels cheap, unearned and an easy way to show an entity’s power.

If you really want to continue working on this concept, you will need to add a narrative to explain the scp’s origins, goals or unique containment procedures. How was it created? Why is it so disappointed by people it encounters? More interestingly, perhaps, how does the Foundation plan on containing a scip like this? Will it take ten industrious teenagers studying in plain sight for it to be pacified?

If you decide to revise the concept / respond below, do drop me another PM and I’ll do my best to take another look at it. For now, all the best! You definitely have my sympathies.

item.content:encoded:
Summoned via PM:

Hi again jpdelta6. Let’s take a look at your new concept.

Okay, I agree with everything Grigori Karpin is saying – basically, we need to work on building a narrative within your existing concept. Basically, you can’t just have a cool idea and inspiration for a scp these days – you have to show us how it works through the eyes of other characters within your article.

For example, what you’ve listed under “Central Narrative” is really you just describing the scp in more detail and how it functions. That’s not a story. A story involves a character encountering problems and trying to solve then. So, to give you an example:

“A shy college dormitory student discovers an unbranded cylinder Bluetooth stereo one day. He plays it in his room, and suddenly, he becomes the most popular student on campus, with people flocking to his room to party day and night… Little does he realise his strength fading day by day, and he starts to hear mysterious voices calling payment for his soul.”

Do you see how I’ve merely focused on a small aspect of your scip and turned it into a compelling discovery log? You can expand on this on choose another area to focus on. But we need to see a narrative in your articles before most of us are willing to greenlight concepts.

If you decide to revise the concept / respond below, do drop me another PM and I’ll do my best to take another look at it. For now, all the best!

item.title: SCP Concept: Life is short
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: A humanoid SCP that is given birth to by a randomly picked woman in labour across the world, however the SCP will only live for 24 hours and when it dies another woman gives birth to it. It varies gender between times.

Central Narrative: A woman is in a hospital, going through labour, and finally gives birth to her child. She's happy, but something feels off, the child doesn't scream and both her and the doctors are shocked and panicked, until the baby speaks to them and wiggles itself free. When on the ground, it introduces itself to them before being taken to a special room in the hospital. The child doesn't understand them and tries to leave the room before being studied by doctors, amongst them an undercover Field Agent from the Foundation. It soon explains itself to the team and it's able to escape from the hospital. After that it seeks new places to go, observe, study and learn. This SCP was then reported to the Foundation and later was observed and studied a few times by the Staff.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The most interesting thing about this anomaly is that the SCP can remember past life experiences, it can grow very intelligent and wise over years and aqquire knowledge for many things, even as a newborn, and it's believed that it's main purpose is to learn. The only limits it has is it's very short life and it's physical form when both very young and very old. The SCP is also never born with any defficiency. What's also interesting about this SCP is that currently it poses no threats to humans, however, as it grows more intelligent there is a possibility of it attempting to end humans.

Additional Notes: Some of the SCP's origin was discovered in a few interviews the Foundation had with it, it was discovered who it's first birth mother was and when it was created. The SCP also explains it's theory in how and why this anomaly was made and how it is yet to discover how to stop it. The anomaly is normally calm during interviews and shows no interest in harm of any life form, however it is triggered when reminded it has a short life cycle.

Her theory claims that there is in fact an SCP inside of SCP-XXXX, an SCP that has the ability to alter or block the formation of memories of anyone that is aware of it to not include it, and it is likely that whoever brought this SCP in has already lost all memories of how they did it, containing it in an anomalous cell just before all their memories were gone as a last-ditch effort in containing it.

item.title: The Copy - Idea
item.content:encoded:
Nickname: "The Copy".
Class: Safe Euclid

I've always had an interest in writing and I've have been writing for a couple years now, on an app called Wattpad. My writing has flaws but bare with me please. And let me know if an idea like it has already been used, I'd hate to feel as if someone already had the idea and I was taking it.

"Copy" is a very strange female humanoid with charcoal coloured skin around the head and neck. The rest fades into very pale and normal skin. It's hair is pure white and it has no recognizable facial features, even when direct light is on it's face. It's movements are slow but, despite it's lack of eyes, seems to know exactly where it is going.

Copy was found standing on a bridge near an extremely old forest. It made no effort to run or even hide from personnel. However, once they were close enough, It slowly pointed to a particularly dark clearing in the distance of the forest. Upon investigating, a body of a female was found wearing the exact same clothes as Copy (a stripped shirt falling off her shoulders and a light grey, 2 tier skirt). The body's skull had been removed but the rest of the body was still there. The identity of the corpse couldn't be discovered but it's killer was nearby and terminted. It was apprehended and brought in for questioning. However, to question it, you need to spend longer than necessary with it, as explained below.

The most unique thing about Copy is the way it manages to speak. While it cannot speak on it's own terms, it can mimic another person's facial features (including skin) and voice. The face is copied while it's hair and the rest of it's body remains the same. To answer the Foundation's questions, she will copy the face and words said to her in the exact tone and pitch of the person in front of her. This lead to quite a bit of irritation when talking to it, unless you are not easily angered, as the foundation had no idea how to get answers out of it. Than all of a sudden it spoke back, answering as many questions as it could with the words it's interviewer spoke. The way it spoke back is by using the words spoken to her, just chopped up (think of video game modders, occasionally they have to cut up NPC dialogue to make voices), to make legible sentences. The issue is that once the interviewer has stopped talking to it, it removes any source of conversation it previously had with the interviewer, so no matter how long the foundation spoke with Copy, she would always forget. And if too many people are speaking at once, she will manage to form all faces on it's face and overlap all the words speaking.

On quite a few occasions, 073 was the one to be sent to question it, due to his genuine friendliness and calm personality. 073
spent 3 hours speaking to Copy and had quite a few questions answered. I imagine it like this:

073: Hello
Copy: Hello
073: How are you?
Copy: How are you?
073: Are you…Copying me?
Copy: Are you…Copying me?
073: Okay…What's your name?
Copy: Copy. What's your name?
073: Cain, or 073, if you prefer
Copy: Cain
073: Yes, that's my name
Copy: How are you?

Or something like that. I imagine if you talk enough than it is more than happy to talk back.

It isn't at all aggressive towards personnel and quite passive about aggressive things that are said to it. It's interesting to watch people insult it for the insult to bounce back at them.

I set it to Euclid because when a breach occurs, she flips out, destroying her containment cell and anyone who enters while this is happening. So far, I'd imagine only a small amount of lives cover her hands, so when she appears agitated, just leave her be until she literally knocks herself out.

it looked like it would take months

Like Zyn mentioned, strong ideas tend to attract more crit faster (so silence can itself be an indicator that an idea might need improving) but it's worth mentioning good writing frequently does take ages; it's a process more than an act. If you check the comments section, author's notes for many SCPs mention months or even years of off-and-on development.

You'll see the occasional bolt-of-inspiration idea thrown together over a weekend, but that's the exception, not the rule.

item.title: Re: Time: Limited
item.content:encoded:
One thing I learned real early writing on the wiki is that there's a direct trade-off between mystery and amount of story told, and your way too far to one side of that equation.

Regarding your specific idea, you're thinking way, way too small. There's barely anything happening here. If you think about this like a movie, you've got the pre-credits scene, maybe the first act if we're being generous. They detect a signal, do exactly what you would expect them to, and we discover some extremely vague mysterious info about the threat. There's nowhere near enough there for us readers to sink our teeth into, so we aren't going to care enough to fill in the gaps and be scared.

You need to ask yourself at least three really big What next?'s. And I'm not talking small answers, like "the mass is quivering." I'm talking big answer, like "IT GETS HERE" big, or "we discover some really cool or strange unexpected thing about the senders/object/universe" big. That is the scale you're operating on with extraterrestrial SCPs.

Like, in terms of existing SCPs, sometimes the answer to that question was "we find a planet that died as a god was born and all that's left is its massive corpse", or "there was an entire civilisation that was deeply inspired by us and died out, but wanted to thank us", or "ancient humanity slew aliens and destroyers a giant geodesic sphere around Earth," or "the signal led to an invasion of earth so bad that we had to put 055 in 579, told in a dozen successive documents."

(Each of those had mysterious elements as well.)

BIG answers.

Push yourself. A lot. You've barely started.

item.title: Re: [Looking for Greenlights] Gaining Perspective - SCP Article
item.content:encoded:
None, save for a development in research methods and a technical exoneration.

So like, what happens here? What research methods are developed? Who is exonerated and why?

This particular concept hones in on a mix of scopophobia, schizophrenia, and paranoia; the irrational anxieties related to being cosmically spied on.

How are you going to like,,,convey this? Like, these are definitely evocative and there's definitely a lot of ways you can really show this by telling a story with characters in the SCP format but I don't really have a feel for how you're intending doing it.

At the end of the day, I don't dislike this as an idea, but I don't feel like I have anywhere near enough of an idea of what you're going to do here to be comfortable greenlighting this.
